discovery: Invention and development of the optical lattice atomic clock

nominees.name: Hidetoshi Katori
nominees.affiliation: University of Tokyo and RIKEN, Japan

nominees.name: Jun Ye
nominees.affiliation: JILA, NIST and University of Colorado Boulder, USA

subfield: Atomic, molecular and optical physics / precision measurement
motivation: Katori proposed and demonstrated the optical lattice clock: neutral atoms trapped at a 'magic' wavelength where the trapping light shifts both clock levels equally, so that many atoms can be interrogated without perturbing the transition. Ye turned this idea into the world's most precise and accurate clocks, reaching fractional uncertainties near 10^-18 and beyond through spin-resolved control of many-body interactions, ultrastable lasers and imaging spectroscopy. Together they improved timekeeping by about two orders of magnitude beyond cesium standards. These clocks have created a new measurement paradigm. They measure the gravitational redshift over height differences from centimetres down to a millimetre, they enable relativistic geodesy, and they provide sensitive searches for dark matter and for variations of fundamental constants. They are also driving the redefinition of the SI second. This is a decisive advance in precision measurement, with both fundamental and practical impact.
